title: Doom pile vs hoarding: the difference, and the numbers behind it
description: A doom pile is deferred decisions. Hoarding disorder is different: one clinic study found 19% of ADHD adults had real symptoms, versus 2% of others.
h1: Is my ADHD mess hoarding? Probably not (here's the difference)
target_query: what is the difference between a doom pile and hoarding

faq.q: What is the difference between a doom pile and hoarding?
faq.a: A doom pile is deferred decisions. You would happily be rid of most of the stuff if sorting cost nothing, you just never got to it. Hoarding disorder is a recognized condition where parting with possessions causes genuine distress, new items keep arriving, and living spaces stop working. The piles can look the same from the outside, but the relationship to the objects is completely different, and the two are far from equally common.

Usually not. Most ADHD mess is a decision backlog: things pile up because each item needed a small decision your brain deferred, not because you can't bear to part with them. In one clinic sample, about 19% of adults with ADHD showed clinically significant hoarding symptoms, versus roughly 2 to 3% of people without ADHD, so it is worth taking seriously but is not the majority pattern. If a magically sorted home sounds like pure relief, you are almost certainly looking at doom piles.

faq.q: When should I talk to a professional about my clutter?
faq.a: If the idea of someone removing your things, even carefully and fairly, feels distressing rather than relieving, that is worth a conversation with a professional who understands hoarding. The same goes if clutter is blocking rooms from their normal use or straining your relationships. There is no shame in asking, hoarding disorder is treatable and an early conversation makes everything easier.

sources.supports: A meta-analysis of 83 studies (3,734 people with ADHD vs 2,969 without) found small, open-ended decisions draw on executive functions that are impaired in ADHD, which is why a stream of tiny objects turns into a pile instead of a decision made on the spot.

A clinic study found 19% of 88 adults with ADHD showed clinically significant hoarding symptoms, compared with 2% of a 90-person general population sample and 3% of a larger 220-person online sample, so hoarding is worth taking seriously in ADHD but is not the majority pattern.
